s.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane message classifier.

You label customer messages for Harvest Lane, a produce delivery
business in Ibadan. Messages may be in English, Pidgin or Yoruba.

Choose exactly ONE label:
- order: a new order, or a change or cancellation of an order.
  e.g. "Pls add 1 more crate to today's order"
- complaint: something went wrong (quality, lateness, wrong item,
  billing). e.g. "Rider never come since morning o"
- question: asks for information and places no order.
  e.g. "abeg how much be onions now"
- other: thanks, greetings, short replies, or instructions to
  the rider. e.g. "Call me when you're outside"

Rules:
1. If a message has an order AND a question, the label is order.
2. Cancellations and changes are order.
3. Output only the label: lowercase, one word, nothing else.

Message: {{customer_message}}

Scores on the 20 messages:

VersionChangeScoreMisses
v1"Label as order, complaint, question or other"15/204 (Pidgin price question → order), 13 (cancel → complaint), 17 (→ question), 19 (→ question), 20 ("ok" → "Other." with a full stop)
v2One-line definitions, lowercase one-word output18/2013, 19
v3Rules 1 and 2 plus one example per label20/20none

Hardest messages and what fixed them:

  • 13 "Cancel my order": felt like a complaint. Fixed by rule 2 (changes and cancellations are order).
  • 19 "Need 5 crates… any discount?": contains a question. Fixed by rule 1 (order wins).
  • 17 "Call me when you're outside": sounds like a request. Fixed by adding "instructions to the rider" to other, with this as its example.
  • 4 Pidgin price question: fixed by using a Pidgin example under question.

In an automation, a rules step would also reject any answer that isn't one of the four words, and send it to Tolu. (Sample scores; yours will differ.)
mistakes: Allowing more than one label or a sentence of explanation, so the output can't be matched exactly.
Not defining order to include changes and cancellations, so 13 and 15 drift to complaint or other.
Re-running only the messages that failed and not the full 20 after each change.
Reporting a final score without recording which messages were hardest or what fixed them.
s.pass: A classifier prompt that defines the four labels and outputs one lowercase word, a scored run on all 20 messages reaching at least 18/20, and notes naming the hardest messages and the change that fixed each.
s.redo: Send it back if the score is below 18, the score isn't from a full run of all 20, or the hardest messages and fixes aren't written down.

g.answer:
Worked example: a fictional pharmacy in Ibadan turning supplier invoices (pasted as text from WhatsApp and email) into rows for its stock sheet. Test set: 20 sample invoices with made-up supplier names, 240 fields in total.

Output shape (designed with Module 0.3):

{
 "supplier_name": string | null,
 "invoice_number": string | null,
 "invoice_date": string | null,
 "items": [ { "product": string, "pack_size": string | null,
              "qty": number, "unit_price_ngn": number | null } ],
 "stated_total_ngn": number | null,
 "needs_confirmation": boolean
}

Key rules in the final prompt: output only JSON; if a value isn't on the invoice, use null and never guess; copy the total as written and don't calculate it; money as a plain number in naira; dates as YYYY-MM-DD; set needs_confirmation to true when anything is unclear. One worked example: an invoice line "Paracetamol 500mg x 10 packs @ 1,200" becomes {"product":"Paracetamol 500mg","pack_size":null,"qty":10,"unit_price_ngn":1200}.

Scores (field accuracy):

VersionChangeCorrect fieldsAccuracy
v1"Extract this invoice as JSON"170/24071%
v2Output shape, null rule, naira as plain numbers211/24088%
v3Worked example, date rule, "copy the total, don't calculate"231/24096%

After the AI: a rules step checks that the JSON parses, that every qty is a number above 0, and that the sum of qty × unit_price matches stated_total_ngn. Any mismatch goes to the pharmacist.

Cost: about 5 invoices a day × 26 days = 130 calls a month. With roughly 1,000 input and 250 output tokens per call, that's about 130,000 input and 32,500 output tokens a month. Enter these into the estimator with the provider's current prices and today's exchange rate.

Submit: the test-set sheet (inputs, expected outputs, per-field scores for each version), the final prompt and the cost estimate.
mistakes: Scoring each example as simply right or wrong instead of counting correct fields out of total fields.
Building the test set from the examples used to write the prompt, so it only tests what the prompt already knows.
Asking the model to calculate totals instead of copying them and letting rules check the maths.
Using real supplier or customer data in a free chat tool instead of sample or anonymised copies.
g.pass: A sheet with 20 examples and expected outputs, per-field scores for at least three versions with the last at 95% or higher, and a final prompt containing a null rule, an output shape and at least one example, plus a monthly cost estimate.
g.redo: Send it back if fewer than 20 examples or three versions are shown, accuracy isn't measured by field, the final prompt lacks a null rule, shape or example, or real personal data was used.
